name: Men's rights movement
summary: The men's rights movement holds that law, courts and social institutions disadvantage men and boys, and campaigns on issues such as child custody and child support, false accusations, male-only conscription, domestic violence against men, male suicide and health, and routine infant circumcision. It generally rejects feminism and the claim that society systematically privileges men. It is a loose, largely online and single-issue movement with no economic or wider political programme.
scope: The contemporary English-language men's rights movement as described on Wikipedia and in coverage of its conferences, drawing on its fathers' rights groups, A Voice for Men and Warren Farrell's work. Because it has no doctrine beyond gender issues, most answers outside gender, family and conscription are low-confidence. It excludes the earlier men's liberation movement, and the separatist MGTOW and pickup-artist strands are noted only as variants.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The movement does not take a stance on healthcare systems; it only complains about funding gaps such as prostate cancer research versus women's health, which cuts both ways.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: No documented position; the movement's economic concerns are about alimony, child support and sentencing, not wage floors.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Activists span libertarian and centrist views and the movement has no economic doctrine; no stance is documented.

public-ownership.rationale: Nothing in the movement's issue lists touches ownership of industry; adherents are split along general political lines.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: No stated position; adherents' tax views vary with their general politics, not their men's-rights stance.

unions-good.rationale: The movement does not address unions; its concerns are family courts and state services, so no position can be inferred.

property-fundamental.rationale: Not a topic in the movement's literature, though complaints about alimony and asset division in divorce hint at some property sympathy; adherents are split.

regulate-corporations.rationale: No documented position on corporate regulation; the movement targets government and feminism, not business.

cut-welfare.rationale: Activists criticise welfare and child support as favouring women, but also demand men's services and benefits, so there is no clear line.

worker-ownership.rationale: Not addressed by the movement; no basis for a position.

surveillance-ok.rationale: No documented stance on surveillance; adherents vary.

legalize-drugs.rationale: The movement has no drug policy beyond complaints about harsher male sentencing; adherents are split.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Activists present themselves as victims of censorship and labelling as hate (for example the SPLC listing) and oppose speech codes, but this is inferred rather than a stated plank.

strong-leader.rationale: No stated view on executive power; the movement is oriented to courts and legislation, not leadership.

state-harmful.rationale: The movement criticises state bias but demands state action (shelters, ministries for men, legal reform), so it is not anti-statist; inferred from its policy demands.

limit-guns.rationale: No movement position; adherents differ by national and political background.

empower-police-military.rationale: No stated position; the movement's grievance about police concerns domestic-violence arrest policies rather than overall funding.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Not a core issue and adherents are split between sexual-liberty and traditionalist views.

rehabilitation.rationale: The movement complains of harsher sentences for men but has no stated penal philosophy.

traditional-family.rationale: Fathers' rights wings stress fathers' involvement and shared parenting, but the movement also attacks marriage law as unfair to men and MGTOW rejects marriage; adherents are genuinely split.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: No stated position; the movement is not organised around this issue.

abortion-legal.rationale: The movement debates male reproductive choice ('paper abortion') and paternal notification, but has no shared view on legality of abortion itself.

more-religion-public.rationale: No stated position; adherents mix secular online activists and religious fathers' groups.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: The movement has no stance on racial redress; its framing of disadvantage is about sex.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Activists dispute feminist claims that gender roles are imposed, and some cite innate sex differences, though the sources describe this only in passing; adherents vary.

gradual-change.rationale: The movement seeks policy reform through courts and legislatures but has no stated view on pace of change.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The movement is hostile to UN Women and similar bodies it sees as feminist-led (UN Women lists men's rights among 'anti-rights' movements), so adherents are inferred to resist more power for them.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: No documented position, though some manosphere strands are technology-optimistic; inferred as split.

revolution-justified.rationale: The movement works through advocacy, lawsuits and legislation and distances itself from violence in its public statements; inferred from its methods.

experts-over-public.rationale: Activists distrust academics, social workers and family-court professionals they see as biased against men, and say research is skewed by feminism; inferred.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Nothing in the movement suggests abolishing wages; its grievance about men being valued as providers implies work-and-pay is taken for granted.

one-party-rule.rationale: The movement operates in democratic politics, lobbying legislatures, and has no stated claim for single-party rule; inferred.

democracy-best.rationale: The movement operates within democratic politics but also contains strands that reject electoral participation (MGTOW) or women's suffrage rhetoric; AVFM disavows the latter. No clear position.

natural-rulers.rationale: Mainstream adherents claim equality for men not rule by a natural elite; critics allege male supremacy in some groups, but the typical adherent claims equal treatment.

political-violence-never.rationale: Public statements of main groups stress non-violent advocacy, though the SPLC cites inflammatory material from some; inferred agree for the typical adherent.

war-builds-character.rationale: The movement treats men as expendable in war ('male disposability') and objects to being sent to fight, so it is unlikely to glorify war.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The movement is largely secular and online; no scripture-based programme is documented, though some religious fathers' groups exist.

private-courts-defense.rationale: No documented position; the movement wants family courts reformed rather than privatised.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The movement frames the key conflict as one between the sexes, with men as the disadvantaged side, not as class struggle; inferred.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Activists often reject equality-of-outcome measures such as pay-gap policy and say disparities reflect choices, while demanding equal legal treatment; inferred.

self-interest-moral.rationale: No documented position; the movement frames its aims as justice, though MGTOW emphasises male self-interest.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Activists present their case as one of rights and equal treatment (conscription, custody) and object to duties imposed on men alone, such as the draft and child support.

restore-past-order.rationale: Critics such as Allan call the movement reactionary and others say it opposes a more equal gender order, but adherents claim to seek equality, not restoration; split.

direct-action.rationale: The main groups use lobbying, litigation, conferences and online publishing rather than direct action, though A Voice for Men has run provocative campaigns; inferred.

return-to-foraging.rationale: No sign of primitivism in the movement.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: No connection to Marxism is documented; the movement rejects class-based dictatorship frames; inferred.

taxation-theft.rationale: No documented position, though some libertarian-leaning adherents say so; split.

harm-principle.rationale: No stated view; adherents want legal protection from false accusations and compelled child support but are split on broader state limits.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The movement claims equal individual rights for men and boys and targets group-based preferences for women, but also advocates sex-based categories such as 'men's rights' and fathers' groups; split.

conscription.rationale: The male-only draft is one of the movement's standard grievances, framed as sex discrimination and a sign of male disposability.

exit-over-voice.rationale: MGTOW stresses withdrawal from society but this is not about leaving a country; no position.

media-academia-power.rationale: Activists commonly claim that academia and media are dominated by feminist perspectives that marginalise men's issues, which a Hatewatch report on a men's issues conference reflects in its account of speakers.

hereditarian-race.rationale: No documented position; race is not part of the movement's issue list.

total-state.rationale: The movement criticises state overreach in family and criminal law and does not seek a state directing all of life; inferred.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: No sign of feudal ideas in the movement.

bound-labor.rationale: The movement objects to compulsory burdens on men (draft, child support), so bound labour is inferred as opposed.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Activists appeal to neutral statistics and research on male disadvantage while accusing feminist scholarship of bias, which implies a belief in objective knowledge; inferred.

school-vouchers.rationale: No documented position, though some activists want single-sex classes and alternatives to mainstream schooling for boys; split.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Online strands often present themselves as rationalist, but religious fathers' groups exist; no shared position.

work-for-welfare.rationale: No documented position, though the movement criticises benefits systems for favouring women; split.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Mainstream adherents demand equal legal treatment of men (custody, conscription, domestic-violence services) and attack sex-based legal distinctions, though some strands are traditionalist; the core framing is anti-discrimination.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Race segregation is not part of the movement and its rights-based framing opposes legal classification by group; inferred.

state-class-instrument.rationale: The movement sees the state as biased by sex (towards women), not as an instrument of a ruling class; inferred.

elite-replacement.rationale: No documented position; some manosphere figures touch this theme but it is not part of the movement's agenda.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Activists say patriarchy is a myth and that women hold as much or more power than men; the movement's premise is that men are not privileged relative to women.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: No documented position, though activists distrust politicians they see as pandering to feminist lobbies; split.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: The movement stresses bodily autonomy and paternal reproductive choice and opposes coercion; eugenic policy is inferred to be rejected.

night-watchman-state.rationale: No documented position; the movement seeks state action on family law and male services, but adherents include libertarians.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Not part of the movement; its stated aims do not include discouraging mixed relationships.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Equality before the law between men and women is the movement's stated basis, though critics say some strands treat women as lesser; typical adherent claims equal rights.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: No documented position, though Indian men's groups campaign against laws they see as biased, such as anti-dowry law; no stance on religion-based personal law.

population-transfer.rationale: Not part of the movement; inferred to be opposed given its rights framing.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: No documented position, though some manosphere strands endorse competition; split.

vanguard-party.rationale: The movement is decentralised and has no vanguard organisation.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Activists complain about loss of due-process protections for accused men, and the movement wants those protections strengthened; inferred opposed to suspending them.

party-controls-media.rationale: Activists claim media bias against men and want their views heard, not state control; inferred.

clerical-rule.rationale: No sign of clerical politics in the movement.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: No documented position, though adherents object to male-only conscription.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Activists say they are censored and oppose speech restrictions; inferred.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: No sign of this in the movement.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: No documented position, though activists criticise academia; split.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Activists blame the 'feminization' of schooling for harming boys and criticise gender-equality curricula as one-sided; sex education itself is not a stated issue.

restrict-pornography.rationale: No documented position; adherents are split between libertarian and traditionalist views.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Activists oppose routine infant circumcision, which many religious communities practise, but the movement states no general view on religious exemptions from law.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The movement stresses liberties and due process for men; inferred opposed.

sacred-ruler.rationale: No sign of this in the movement.

character-from-environment.rationale: Activists often cite innate sex differences against feminist environmental accounts, though the sources mention this thinly; inferred.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The movement's rights framing and demands for equal treatment under law imply no one stands above the law; inferred.

decide-locally.rationale: The movement has no stated view on devolution; its demands target national family, criminal and education law.

equal-parenting.rationale: Default equal or joint custody is the central demand of the fathers' rights wing, the main route into the movement.

missingStatements.text: Courts should presume that children of separated parents spend equal time with each parent.
missingStatements.rationale: Joint custody as the default is the central demand of the fathers' rights wing, the main route into the movement.

missingStatements.text: Men and women should be treated identically in law on military conscription.
missingStatements.rationale: The male-only draft is framed as sex discrimination by the movement; adherents want it ended or extended to women.
missingStatements.declined: The existing conscription statement covers the draft question and a male-only-draft statement is too narrow to keep the bank lean.

missingStatements.text: Routine circumcision of infant boys for non-medical reasons should be banned.
missingStatements.rationale: Most members oppose it and compare it to female genital mutilation, and bodily autonomy is a listed issue area.
missingStatements.declined: Infant circumcision is a narrow single-issue topic with low salience across ideologies.

missingStatements.text: A man should be able to avoid legal parenthood for a child he did not choose to father, including by testing paternity or opting out before birth.
missingStatements.rationale: Paternity testing, relief from support for non-biological children and 'paper abortion' are advocated, with paternity listed among core issues.
missingStatements.declined: Paternity opt-out and "paper abortion" is a niche demand within the movement; too narrow for the bank.

missingStatements.text: Women's violence against men in intimate relationships is as significant as men's violence against women and deserves equal shelter and services.
missingStatements.rationale: Activists claim near-symmetry in domestic violence and campaign for shelters for abused men.

notes: Fringe strands (MGTOW, red pill) and the groups the SPLC listed as male supremacist would answer gender questions more extremely; critics argue the movement is defined by backlash against feminism. Almost every non-gender answer is an inference, so the profile may fail the salience check.
